parts.problem_md: Explain **one **advantage to a business of using a time based payment method.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of time-based pay is that it helps the business maintain consistent quality standards **[1]**. Workers are paid for the hours they work rather than the number of units they produce, so they have no financial incentive to rush **[1]**. This reduces the risk of defective products or careless work that can occur with piece rate **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Time-based pay is simple for the business to calculate and administer
> - Time-based pay helps the business maintain consistent quality standards
> - Time-based pay allows the business to plan and control its labour costs effectively
> - Time-based pay gives the business flexibility to increase output through overtime when needed
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Because wages are calculated simply by multiplying hours worked by the hourly rate, the business spends less time on payroll administration, reducing overhead costs and the risk of errors in pay calculations
> - Unlike piece rate, where workers are financially incentivised to work as fast as possible, time-based pay removes the pressure to rush; this reduces the risk of defective output and rework costs, protecting the business's reputation for quality
> - The business can set standard working hours and forecast its weekly wage bill with confidence, making budgeting and financial planning more straightforward and reliable
> - If demand rises unexpectedly, the business can offer overtime to existing workers, increasing output quickly without the cost and disruption of recruiting additional staff
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **benefit to a business of having motivated employees.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit to a business of having motivated employees is lower staff turnover **[1]**. Employees who feel engaged, valued, and satisfied in their work are less likely to leave and look for jobs elsewhere **[1]**. This means the business spends less time and money on recruiting and training replacements, which can be costly and disruptive **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Motivated employees are less likely to be absent from work
> - Motivated employees are less likely to leave the business, resulting in lower staff turnover
> - Motivated employees tend to produce higher-quality products or services
> - Motivated employees provide better customer service
> - Motivated employees are more likely to work towards the business's objectives
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Lower absenteeism means fewer disruptions to production or service delivery, and the business spends less on covering absent workers with temporary or agency staff
> - Lower staff turnover reduces the time and money spent on recruiting and training replacements, and allows the business to retain experienced workers whose skills and knowledge are difficult to replace quickly
> - Employees who take pride in their work produce fewer defective products and generate fewer customer complaints, protecting the business's reputation and reducing the cost of reworking or replacing faulty output
> - Better customer service leads to more repeat customers and positive word-of-mouth recommendations, increasing revenue without additional marketing expenditure
> - When employees are motivated, their personal goals align more closely with those of the business, making it more likely that targets for sales, productivity, or quality will be met
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **advantage to employees of performance-related pay.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of PRP to employees is that it rewards hard work and strong performance with higher pay **[1]**. Employees who meet or exceed their targets receive a bonus on top of their basic salary, meaning their earnings directly reflect the effort and quality they put into their work **[1]**. Many employees see this as fairer than a fixed pay system where everyone earns the same regardless of performance, and this sense of being fairly rewarded increases job satisfaction and motivates them to continue working to a high standard **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - PRP directly rewards employees who work hard and exceed their targets with higher pay
> - PRP is seen by many employees as a fairer system, since pay reflects individual effort and contribution rather than simply time worked
> - PRP gives employees a clear incentive to develop their skills and demonstrate their capabilities
> - PRP allows employees in roles where output cannot be counted in units, such as management,to be financially rewarded for the quality of their work
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Earning more through strong performance allows employees to better meet their financial needs and improve their standard of living, increasing their overall satisfaction with the job
> - Employees who feel their pay reflects their individual contribution are more likely to feel valued and fairly treated compared to a fixed pay system where all workers earn the same regardless of effort or results
> - High performance recognised through PRP can increase an employee's chances of promotion, providing career development opportunities beyond the immediate financial reward
> - For employees in supervisory or management roles, PRP offers a way to be rewarded for the quality and impact of their work, which cannot easily be measured in quantitative terms
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
'Financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business.'

Evaluate this view.
parts.solution_md:
Financial incentives include commission, bonuses, profit sharing, and performance-related pay. In retail, individual performance can often be measured through sales figures, making commission straightforward to implement — staff who sell more earn more, directly linking effort to reward. This is consistent with Taylor's economic man theory, which argues workers are primarily motivated by financial gain. For full-time sales staff in higher-value retail environments such as electronics or furniture stores, the prospect of a meaningful bonus can be a powerful driver of performance and focus.

However, Herzberg's two-factor theory challenges this view. Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor — sufficient pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine motivation. Once retail employees earn enough to meet their basic needs, additional bonuses are unlikely to make them significantly more engaged. True motivators are intrinsic to the job: recognition, responsibility, achievement, and development opportunities. A retail employee given responsibility for training new staff or managing a product range is more likely to feel genuinely motivated than one who receives a modest monthly bonus.

Commission can also undermine teamwork and service quality in retail by encouraging staff to prioritise their own individual sales over helping colleagues or building customer relationships. Many retail workers are part-time, and for them flexible hours and a positive team environment may be more motivating than financial incentives — a point supported by Mayo's human relations theory.

Overall, financial incentives are most effective for sales-focused roles where individual performance is measurable and employees are primarily income-driven. For the broader retail workforce — particularly part-time and customer service staff — non-financial motivators are likely to be equally or more effective. The most successful approach combines fair base pay to prevent dissatisfaction with non-financial motivators that address higher-order needs, creating genuine long-term engagement rather than short-term performance gains alone

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **5** | 17-20 | - Effective evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business |
> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of employee motivation and/or financial motivators |
> 
> **Indicative content **
> 
> - Financial incentives are rewards that motivate employees through money, e.g. commission, bonuses, profit sharing, performance-related pay, piece rate
> - Non-financial motivators are approaches that improve motivation without direct pay increases, e.g. recognition, job enrichment, responsibility, promotion opportunities, a positive working environment
> 
> **For financial incentives in retail**
> 
> - In retail, individual performance can often be measured through sales figures, conversion rates, or customer satisfaction scores, making commission and performance-related pay straightforward to implement; staff who sell more earn more, directly linking effort to reward and encouraging higher productivity - consistent with Taylor's economic man theory, which argues workers are primarily motivated by financial gain
> - Bonuses for hitting weekly or monthly targets give retail employees a clear, tangible goal to work towards; for full-time sales staff in higher-value retail environments (e.g. electronics, car sales), the prospect of a significant bonus may be a powerful driver of performance and focus
> - Profit sharing gives all retail employees a financial stake in the store's success, aligning their interests with those of the business and encouraging a collective effort to improve sales and reduce waste
> 
> **Against — non-financial motivators may be more effective**
> 
> - Herzberg's two-factor theory argues that pay is a hygiene factor rather than a true motivator - sufficient pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine engagement; once retail employees earn enough to meet their basic needs, additional financial incentives are unlikely to make them significantly more motivated; true motivators, such as recognition, responsibility, achievement and personal development - are intrinsic to the job itself, not financial
> - Commission can undermine teamwork and customer service quality by creating a competitive culture in which staff prioritise their own individual sales at the expense of helping colleagues or building long-term customer relationships - particularly damaging in retail environments where consistent service and repeat custom matter
> - Many retail employees are part-time workers, including students, for whom flexible working hours, a positive working environment, and social interaction with colleagues may be more important motivators than financial incentives; Mayo's human relations theory suggests that feeling valued and being part of a supportive team can motivate employees as effectively as financial reward
> - Maslow's hierarchy suggests that once basic financial needs are met, higher-order needs - belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation - become more important; retail managers and long-term employees seeking career development may respond more strongly to promotion opportunities and recognition than to bonuses
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - Financial incentives are most effective in retail roles where individual performance is measurable and employees are primarily income-driven - such as full-time sales staff in high-value environments; they are less effective in roles requiring teamwork, empathy, and consistent customer care
> - Herzberg's research suggests that pay alone will not create lasting motivation - it removes dissatisfaction but does not engage employees with their work in a meaningful way
> - The type of retail employee matters significantly: a commission-driven full-time sales assistant and a part-time student working weekend shifts are unlikely to respond to the same motivational approach
> - The most effective strategy combines fair base pay - meeting hygiene needs and preventing dissatisfaction - with non-financial motivators such as recognition, development opportunities, and a positive team culture that address higher-order needs
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To score highly on this type of question, make sure you structure your answer around both sides of the argument - do not simply list points in favour of financial incentives. The strongest responses will weave in relevant theory (e.g. Herzberg's two-factor theory) and apply it directly to the retail context rather than discussing motivation in general terms.
> 
> A common pitfall is failing to reach a clear judgement at the end. Many students describe arguments for and against but never commit to a conclusion. Your evaluation should explicitly state whether you agree or disagree with the statement, and why - using evidence from your earlier analysis.
> 
> Make sure you apply your answer to retail specifically. Mentioning part-time workers, commission-based sales roles, or customer-facing environments will demonstrate application and help you access the higher mark bands. Avoid generic answers that could apply to any industry.
> 
> Do not spend too long on knowledge recall at the expense of analysis and evaluation - the bulk of the marks (6 out of 12) are for evaluation.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** effect on a business of low employee motivation.
parts.solution_md:
One effect of low employee motivation is higher staff turnover **[1]**. When employees feel undervalued or disengaged, they are more likely to look for work elsewhere and leave the business **[1]**. This forces the business to spend time and money recruiting and training replacements, which increases costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Lower productivity / output per worker
> - Higher rates of absenteeism
> - Higher staff turnover, leading to increased recruitment and training costs
> - Poor quality of work or customer service
> - Reduced creativity and innovation among staff
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If employees lack motivation, they are less likely to work efficiently or take pride in the quality of their output; this can result in higher defect rates, more customer complaints, and potential damage to the business's reputation - particularly in a service business where customer interactions are central to the brand
> - Low motivation often leads to higher absenteeism, which disrupts production schedules or service delivery; if remaining staff must cover for absent colleagues, this adds pressure and may further reduce morale, creating a cycle of declining performance
> - Unmotivated employees are more likely to leave the business in search of more fulfilling or better-paid work; this increases recruitment and training costs, and the business may lose experienced workers whose skills and knowledge are difficult to replace quickly
> - Poor quality of work resulting from low motivation can lead to increased waste, reworking of faulty products, or dissatisfied customers; over time this can harm sales and damage the business's reputation for quality
> - Low motivation reduces employees' willingness to suggest new ideas or find better ways of working; this limits the business's ability to innovate or improve its products and processes, putting it at a competitive disadvantage
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks by simply listing several effects rather than developing one in depth. Focus on a single effect and build a chain of analysis - show how the effect leads to a consequence for the business, and ideally extend this to a further impact (e.g. low motivation → higher absenteeism → disrupted operations → increased costs or lost revenue). Using connective phrases such as "this means that…" or "as a result…" helps demonstrate the analytical thinking examiners are looking for. Avoid vague statements like "the business will do badly" - be specific about the business impact.

**[3 marks]**

Currently, all employees are trained for a single role, creating repetitive work that contributes to declining job satisfaction scores and sharply rising labour turnover (up from 14% to 26% for non-management employees) **[Ap]**. Training employees in a wider range of tasks would make their work more varied and challenging, addressing Herzberg's motivators of the work itself and personal development, which the current system ignores completely **[An]**

MBO is the stronger recommendation at this point **[E]**. It addresses multiple causes of low motivation simultaneously - lack of involvement, poor communication, and no recognition for performance - and fits with the HR Director's recent research **[Ap]** **[E]**. Multi-skilling would also help, but it alone does not tackle the fundamental problem that employees have no voice in how NH is run. Introducing MBO for assistant managers first would be a practical starting point, as their satisfaction has also declined and they are better placed to understand and implement the system before it is rolled out more widely **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Analyse how a business might satisfy the self-actualisation needs of its employees.
parts.solution_md:
Self-actualisation is the highest level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs - the desire to fulfil one's full potential through creative, meaningful, and challenging work **[K]**. One way a business might satisfy these needs is through job enrichment, which involves adding greater responsibility, variety, and challenge to employees' existing roles **[K] [An]**. When employees are given complex or creative tasks that require them to use their full range of skills, they feel they are growing and developing as individuals **[An]**. This increases intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction, making employees more engaged and productive, and reducing the likelihood that they will leave the business to seek more fulfilling work elsewhere **[An]**

A second way is to empower employees by giving them greater autonomy over how they carry out their work **[K]**. For example, allowing creative or specialist teams to make their own decisions - rather than following instructions from managers - satisfies the need for self-expression and personal achievement **[An]**. Employees who feel trusted to direct their own work are more likely to take ownership of outcomes and develop innovative ideas **[An]**. This benefits the business by encouraging creativity and new approaches, which can lead to improved products or processes, while also keeping highly skilled employees motivated and committed to the organisation **[An]**

One new payment method AB could introduce is performance-related pay (PRP) **[K]**. This links each mechanic's earnings to an individual assessment of their performance, rather than simply the hours they work. AB's mechanics have complained that the current time-based system rewards those who take on easy jobs or work slowly just as much as those who work hard on complex repairs **[Ap]**. PRP would address this directly - mechanics who complete more difficult jobs to a higher standard would earn more, making the system fairer. This could increase motivation significantly, as employees would feel that their effort and skill are properly recognised and rewarded **[An]**

A second option is to introduce bonuses **[K]** for mechanics who upsell customers from a standard to an advanced service. AB's directors have identified increasing advanced service sales as a key objective **[Ap]**, and bonuses linked to this outcome would directly incentivise mechanics to recommend the more expensive service where appropriate. parts.problem_md:
*‘The economic man* theory used by Taylor is the best way to motivate the employees of a customer service call centre business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
Taylor's economic man theory argues that workers are motivated primarily by financial reward, and that management should monitor performance closely and link pay directly to output **[K]**

In a customer service call centre, performance can be measured objectively - through call handling times, resolution rates, and sales conversions **[Ap]** - making Taylor's approach feasible **[E]**. Agents could be paid bonuses for hitting measurable targets, and call centres already use technology to monitor activity and record calls **[Ap]**, which is consistent with Taylor's principles of close observation and standardised working methods. For agents motivated primarily by earnings, financial incentives linked to clear targets can be a powerful motivator **[An]**

However, Herzberg's two-factor theory challenges this view. Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor - it prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine motivation **[K]**. In a repetitive and emotionally demanding environment like a call centre, bonuses may reduce dissatisfaction without inspiring agents to deliver empathetic, high-quality service **[Ap] [An]**. True motivators, such as recognition, achievement, and development opportunities, are not addressed by Taylor's approach alone **[E]**

Maslow's hierarchy further suggests that once basic financial needs are met, higher-order needs such as belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation become more important **[K]**. High staff turnover, which is a widespread problem in call centres **[Ap]**, suggests that financial incentives alone are insufficient to retain experienced agents and that non-financial factors play a significant role in long-term motivation **[An]**

Overall, Taylor's theory is only partially correct **[E]**. Financial incentives linked to measurable targets can improve productivity and sales performance, and call centres are well-suited to performance monitoring **[E]**. However, delivering quality customer service requires emotional engagement that financial reward alone cannot fully motivate **[An]**. A combination of Taylor's financial incentives with non-financial motivators, such as recognition, team working, and career development, is likely to produce better results for both employee motivation and the quality of service delivered **[E]**

Non-financial motivators are approaches that do not involve direct pay increases, such as job rotation, team working, and empowerment. Financial motivators use money to incentivise employees, for example through higher wages, deadline bonuses, or performance-related pay **[K]**

Job rotation could reduce the boredom this creates, helping to maintain employee engagement and productivity across the site **[An]**

Team working is another effective non-financial method **[K]**. Construction work naturally involves groups operating together on large projects **[Ap]**, so structuring this formally could build stronger working relationships and raise morale. Maslow's hierarchy of needs suggests that satisfying employees' social needs gives workers a sense of belonging, which encourages them to perform to a higher standard **[An]**

However, financial motivators may be more effective for a large proportion of the workforce. Many construction workers earn modest wages, meaning their basic and safety needs may not be fully met **[K]** **[Ap]**. Taylor's theory suggests that financial reward is the primary motivator for manual workers, which reflects the reality of many roles on a construction site. Deadline bonuses directly link pay to a core business objective and are likely to be more immediately motivating than non-financial approaches for workers focused on their financial security **[An]**

Overall, the statement is only partially correct **[E]**. Lower-paid manual workers, who make up the majority of the workforce in a house building business **[Ap]**, are more likely to respond to financial incentives, particularly when their basic needs are not yet satisfied. Non-financial motivators become more powerful once employees feel financially secure, at which point higher-order needs such as esteem and self-actualisation begin to drive behaviour **[An]**. This means non-financial methods are better suited to site managers and supervisors who already earn enough to meet their basic needs **[Ap]** **[E]**. parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **possible disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees.
parts.solution_md:
Performance-related pay links employees' pay to an assessment of their performance against pre-agreed targets **[K]**. One disadvantage is that it is difficult for a business to measure performance fairly, particularly in roles such as management or customer service **[K] **where output cannot easily be counted. If managers assess employees subjectively, some workers may feel their evaluation was biased or inconsistent **[An]**. This causes employees to lose trust in the system and feel resentful, meaning PRP reduces motivation rather than improving it, working against the very objective the business was trying to achieve **[An]**

A second disadvantage is that PRP can cause conflict between employees **[K]**. Because individuals are rewarded based on their own performance, some workers will earn significantly more than colleagues doing similar work. Those who narrowly miss their targets and receive no bonus may feel undervalued compared to those who do, even if the difference in performance was small **[An]**. This creates jealousy and resentment within teams, damaging cooperation. In a business that depends on employees working together effectively, this breakdown in teamwork could reduce overall productivity **[An] **and actually harm business performance, offsetting any benefits from the individual incentives PRP provides **[An]**

> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
>

> |   |   |   |

> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of performance-related pay and/or motivation |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Performance-related pay (PRP) links an employee's salary or bonus to an assessment of their performance against pre-agreed targets or criteria
> - PRP requires managers to assess whether each employee has met their targets, but in many roles - particularly management and supervisory positions - performance is difficult to measure objectively; if employees feel their assessment was unfair, inconsistent, or influenced by favouritism, they will lose trust in the system and feel demotivated, meaning PRP achieves the opposite of its intended effect and may increase staff grievances or turnover
> - Because PRP rewards individuals based on their own performance, some employees will earn significantly more than colleagues doing similar work; employees who narrowly miss their targets and receive no bonus may feel undervalued compared to those who do, creating resentment and jealousy that damages teamwork and cooperation - in a business that relies on collaborative working, this breakdown in team relations could reduce overall productivity and offset any individual performance gains
> - For employees already working at full capacity, the pressure to meet or exceed targets in order to protect their income can lead to stress, burnout, and higher rates of absenteeism; the business may find that health-related absences increase costs and disrupt output, negating the productivity improvements PRP was designed to create
> - Setting PRP targets that employees consider achievable but stretching is difficult; if targets are set too high, employees may give up trying to reach them, reducing motivation rather than increasing it, while targets that are too easy fail to drive the improvements in performance the business is looking for
>

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **disadvantage of a piece rate payment method.
parts.solution_md:
One disadvantage of piece rate is that workers may rush to complete as many units as possible in order to earn more money **[1]**. This can cause quality standards to fall because workers are focused on speed rather than care **[1]**, which could lead to an increase in defective products and customer complaints **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Workers may rush to complete as many units as possible in order to maximise their earnings
> - If the production line breaks down or materials are unavailable, workers cannot produce units and therefore earn nothing
> - Workers may resist changes to working methods or machinery
> - A competitive atmosphere can develop between workers chasing higher piece rates
> - Piece rate can only be used where output is easily measured and standardised
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Rushing production can cause quality standards to fall or create safety risks, as workers prioritise speed over care
> - The inability to earn during stoppages creates income insecurity and anxiety, which can reduce motivation and morale
> - Workers fear that changes will slow their output and cut their pay, making them unwilling to accept new processes even when these would benefit the business
> - Competition over pay can lead to jealousy, poor teamwork, or higher staff turnover
> - This limits the method's applicability and means it cannot be used for service, knowledge-based, or creative roles
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

For example, do not just write "quality may fall"; go on to explain that workers rushing to maximise output may cut corners, leading to defective products and potential loss of customers.
